intro: Game suggestions from three rounds: the market research, the Idea lab (80 ideas scored and critiqued), and Proven genres (evergreen loops with open themes). Ranked by default for one person building with AI who tests games free in the browser and takes the proven ones to Steam. Switch presets or set your own weights to re-rank.
caveat: No dataset can guarantee a hit, and most games, web or Steam, earn very little. Each suggestion is a bet backed by specific signals, with gates that tell you early whether it's working. The scores are research-based judgements, so treat close scores as ties.

concepts.name: Leaflings
concepts.niche: Make-your-own critters · field-guide collecting · photo-to-creature
concepts.hook: Pick a photo of anything flat (a leaf, a petal, a ticket stub, a crisp). It becomes a little guy.
concepts.oneLiner: Choose a photo of a real flat object and its exact silhouette and colours become a wobbly critter with ink eyes and twig legs, who moves into your herbarium page and fills a field guide of about 30 shape classes.
concepts.pitch: Everyone has a pocket full of little flat things: the maple leaf from the walk home, a cinema ticket, a pressed petal, one perfectly curled crisp. Leaflings turns any of them into a shape-true critter in seconds. You pick a photo from your camera roll (or take one through the phone's own photo sheet), the object peels off the picture, blinks, grows legs and waddles onto a hand-drawn herbarium page. Shapes sort into a field guide of about 30 silhouette classes (maple, ginkgo, heart, needle, ticket, crisp...) with a 6 + 1 secret per season, villagers post a gentle request each morning ('the baker wants something red and pointy'), and every critter can be sent to a friend by link or saved as a sticker. The photo never leaves the phone. No two players own the same creatures, because the creatures come from their own pockets and pavements.

look.short: A kraft-paper herbarium page · real leaves with inked eyes and twig legs
look.vibe: Imagine opening an old botany notebook on a rainy afternoon. Pressed leaves are taped to the cream pages with little handwritten labels, and then one of them blinks. Its edges lift off the paper, two ink-dot eyes open, matchstick legs unfold, and it toddles to the next page to say hello to a ticket stub with a top hat.
look.layout: Portrait phone screen. Top: a slim paper tab with today's villager request in handwriting ('The baker wants something red and pointy') next to the villager's little face, and a row of seasonal silhouettes showing 6 + 1 slots. Middle two-thirds: the herbarium page itself, cream paper with faint ruled lines, where your critters stand, wander and nap beside handwritten labels; swipe sideways to turn pages. Bottom third: a big round 'find' button shaped like a magnifying glass, with 'pick a photo' and 'draw one' as two smaller buttons beside it. When you pick a photo, the page dims, your picture appears like a print on the desk, a dotted line traces around the object, it peels off with a paper rustle, eyes pop open, legs unfold, and the new critter walks onto the page and its silhouette fills in the field guide.
references: Victorian herbarium sheets and pressed-flower books
look.shapes: The body is whatever the player found, kept true to its silhouette; everything added is small and simple: round dot eyes, a tiny curved mouth, thin twig legs, little hats.
look.characters: Critters are 90% real object and 10% personality. Villagers are a handful of round paper-doll neighbours (a baker, a postmistress, a beetle librarian) and a loaf-shaped shop cat.
look.camera: Flat, top-down, like looking at a notebook on a desk. Portrait first, so a screenshot is one full page.
look.lighting: Soft overcast window light, with a gentle drop shadow under each critter so it looks like it's standing on the paper.
look.textures: Kraft and cream paper grain, washi tape corners, pencil ruling, real photo texture on every critter.
look.ui: Paper tabs and torn-edge cards, rubber-stamp icons, big thumb-sized round buttons.
look.type: A handwriting font made from the creator's own handwriting for labels, with a clean serif (e.g. Literata) for the field guide.
look.motion: Critters peel off with a slight curl, wobble when they walk, and do a tiny hop when tapped; pages turn with a real paper bend.
look.sound: Paper rustle, a soft 'pip' when eyes open, tiny twig footsteps, pencil scratches. Music: acoustic guitar and soft woodwinds.
look.screenshot: A full herbarium page: a maple leaf, a ginkgo, a ticket stub and a crisp standing in a row with handwritten labels under each.
look.clip: A hand holds a red maple leaf on white paper → snap → it peels off the photo → eyes open → it waddles onto the page. Five seconds.

Glossy plastic UI or neon colours
Any imitation of a known illustrator's style

concepts.name: If It Fits
concepts.niche: Soft-body physics puzzle · cats are liquid · daily room
concepts.hook: Cats are liquid. Prove it: pour this chonk into a teacup.
concepts.oneLiner: A no-fail soft-body puzzle where you nudge, tip and coax squishy cats into teacups, boxes, boots and sinks until every cat fits and sits, with a new room every morning.
concepts.pitch: 'Cats are liquid' and 'if it fits, I sits' are two of the internet's oldest cat jokes, and nobody has made the game that proves them. In If It Fits each room has a few soft-body cats and some deeply unsuitable containers. You nudge and tip them, and they glorp, ooze and loaf into place. Each breed flows differently (a kitten pours like water, a Persian like honey, a chonk like pudding, a sphynx wobbles like jelly), so breeds are both the puzzle variety and a 6 + 1 secret collection. A new room arrives every morning, generated from a shared prop library and checked by a solver so it always has a fair par, and a sandbox photo room lets players pour any cat into anything and post the result. When the last cat settles, the camera pans over the room as the purring builds. It's a physics clip that sells itself and a perfect portal game.

concepts.hook: Send a secret note. They have to iron it to read it.

concepts.pitch: Group chats are full of words and short on gestures. As you collect stationery, the reveal changes: hold a candle under it, rub a pencil across it, steam it over a kettle. concepts.niche: Houseplant care · gift-by-link · living family trees
concepts.hook: This plant has lived in 4,000 phones. Here's your cutting. Grow it, snip it, pass it on.
concepts.oneLiner: A cozy houseplant game where new plants only arrive as cuttings sent by link, rare mutations appear only in descendants, and every plant carries a family tree back to a public mother plant named in a creator video.
concepts.pitch: Grow a Garden proved that gardening plus rare mutations is the biggest cozy fantasy going, and real plant people already make friends by handing out pothos cuttings in jam jars. Cuttings makes that ritual the whole game: you can't buy or find a plant, only receive one. Every newcomer gets a free cutting from a public mother plant (each creator video names one, like 'Biscuit'), so a stranger from TikTok is growing in seconds and joins one giant visible lineage. Tend it for a minute, snip a cutting when a node is ready, and send it by link. Rare traits (variegated, pink stem, heart leaf, moon leaf...) only ever show up in descendants, so the best plants are always gifts. Per-lineage leaderboards ('Biscuit: generation 31, 12 countries') give group chats something to race on, and milestone reveals ('your cutting now has 100 descendants') are the clip. Plants are drawn by an L-system from about eight hand-drawn leaf shapes, and a light server keeps every plant safe even when iOS wipes browser storage.

look.short: A sunny windowsill of jam-jar cuttings · hand-drawn leaves on living vines
look.vibe: Imagine a sunny apartment windowsill lined with jam jars of water, each holding a trailing green cutting with tiny white roots curling in the glass. You slide a pair of brass scissors across a vine: snip. The cutting drops into a fresh jar with a soft plink, roots wriggle out, and a little kraft-paper gift tag flips over: 'Biscuit · generation 32 · for Sam'. Somewhere off-screen, a family tree grows one more twig.
look.layout: Portrait phone screen. Top: a slim kraft-paper tag showing your plant's lineage ('Biscuit · gen 32 · 4,112 descendants · 23 countries') with a tiny tree icon that opens the family tree. Middle two-thirds: the windowsill seen straight on, your plant in its pot or jar with vines spilling over the edge and soft window light behind; when a node is ready, one small bud glows. Below the sill: big object buttons for care (a watering can, a mister, a turn-the-pot arrow) and a pair of brass scissors. Bottom: a tab bar of Sill, Family tree and Traits (six silhouettes plus one '?' secret). The key interaction: drag the scissors across the glowing node; the cutting falls into a jam jar, roots curl out, and a share sheet slides up with the gift-tag preview to send by link. Opening someone else's link plays it in reverse: a jar arrives on your sill and roots in front of you.
references: Real propagation stations: cuttings in jam jars on a windowsill
Old herbarium labels and seed packets (for layout and labels)
look.shapes: Organic but tidy: rounded leaves with one confident outline, cylindrical jars, chunky terracotta pots. Vines curve in smooth arcs, never jagged or tangled.
look.characters: The plants are the characters: each lineage has a name (Biscuit, Noodle, Pip) and each owner a preset nickname ('Mossy Otter'). Fig, a loaf-shaped tabby, naps between the jars next to its own pot of cat grass.
look.camera: Straight-on, like standing at the window; portrait 9:16 so one screenshot is the whole sill. The family tree zooms out smoothly from a single leaf to the whole lineage.
look.lighting: Daylight through the window follows the player's real clock: cool morning, golden afternoon, lamplit evening. Mutated leaves catch the light softly (variegation glows), never sparkle like a slot machine.
look.textures: Painted leaves with visible brush grain, soft glass refraction on the jars, speckled terracotta, kraft-paper tags on string.
look.ui: Kraft-paper tags and seed-packet cards; big thumb-sized object buttons; a trait card with six silhouettes and one secret, odds printed underneath like a seed packet.
look.type: A warm serif for names and labels (e.g. Fraunces) with a clean sans body (e.g. Nunito); generation numbers in a small typewriter face like a herbarium label.
look.motion: Vines grow with a gentle ease and sway; leaves unfurl; a drooping plant slumps and perks back up with a tiny bounce when watered; roots curl out in the jar.
look.sound: Recorded real sounds: scissors snip, water poured into glass, a jar set on wood, rustling leaves, a cat purr. Music: soft piano and nylon guitar.
look.screenshot: A packed windowsill of jars and pots, one cream-and-green variegated vine trailing down the middle, its gift tag reading 'gen 32'.
look.clip: Extreme close-up of one heart-shaped leaf → fast zoom out through a glowing family tree → '4,112 descendants · 23 countries'. Five to eight seconds.

concepts.name: Fold Together
concepts.niche: Couch co-op · cloth physics · laundry folding for two
concepts.hook: Fold a fitted sheet with your partner. One phone, four thumbs. Try not to bicker.
concepts.oneLiner: A two-player cloth-physics game where each person holds two corners of a floppy sheet, on one phone or on two phones by link, folding a daily basket of three items (one of them absurd) and learning hotel folds that end in towel animals.
concepts.pitch: Every couple has fought over a fitted sheet, and 'cozy games for couples' is one of the most requested and least supplied lanes in the research. Fold Together turns that tiny domestic moment into a calm, untimed co-op toy: each person grabs two corners, you stretch, line up the edges and the cloth snaps into a crisp fold with a soft thwump. There are no fail states, only gentle bickering ('your other left'). A daily basket of three items (one absurd: an octopus costume, a parachute) ends in a shareable fold-score card, a hotel-fold path ends in towel animals (swan, elephant, cat), and your linen closet fills with neat stacks. Play on one phone laid flat between you, on two phones paired by link (for long-distance couples and friends), or as a Discord Activity inside a voice call. Fabrics are scans of real textiles, so the art is human-made by definition.

look.short: A sunny laundry room for two · real scanned fabrics that flop and snap
look.vibe: Imagine a sunlit laundry room with a big pine folding table and a basket of warm, slightly wrinkled washing. A gingham sheet lies between two people; four fingertips pinch its corners, it billows and sags, someone says 'your other left', and then the edges meet and it snaps into a crisp square with a soft thwump and a puff of lavender. look.layout: Same-phone mode: the phone lies flat on the table between you, in portrait. Top end (upside down, facing the far player): their two teal corner rings and a small 'tiny arguments' tally. Middle: the folding table seen from straight above, today's item spread out, with a faint dotted crease guide. Bottom end, facing you: your two coral corner rings and the basket counter (2 of 3), with the absurd item peeking out of the basket. The key interaction: each person presses and drags their two corners; when the edges line up, the crease guide turns gold; let go and the cloth snaps into the fold with a thwump, slides off onto a neat stack at the side, and the next item tumbles out. In online mode each phone shows the table from its own end, and the partner's fingertips appear as soft teal rings.

concepts.name: Driftgarden
concepts.niche: Cozy survival-lite crafting · co-op 1–4 · ocean setting
concepts.oneLiner: Grow a floating garden-boat with up to three friends and sail a flooded, sunlit archipelago. No death, no hunger bars, no rush.
concepts.pitch: The islands have slipped beneath a gentle sea. You and your friends tend a houseboat that is also a garden: plant on the deck, fish over the rail, salvage sunken cottages, and graft new rooms onto the hull as it grows. Each island has a small community to help and a biome to bring back to life. It keeps survival-craft's 'gather, craft, expand, explore' loop, the best-performing niche in the research, removes everything punishing, and is built for co-op from day one.

concepts.artDirection: Bright stylized 3D with a watercolor sea and chunky, readable silhouettes. The capsule should say 'a garden on a boat' at thumbnail size.

concepts.name: Well Loved
concepts.niche: First-person restoration sim · plush toy hospital · keepsakes with stories
concepts.oneLiner: Run a tiny plush hospital: wash, de-pill, stitch and restuff worn, much-loved toys, then hand them back and read what their owners say.
concepts.hook: Fix a child's first bear without erasing the love marks.
concepts.pitch: A first-person, bench-scale restoration game set in a small plush hospital above a high-street shop. Each job arrives in a cardboard box with a note from its owner: a child's first bear with a split seam, a grandmother's rabbit gone flat and grey, a dog's chew toy that's 'part of the family'. You assess the damage, wash it in a basin, shave the pills off in clean stripes, open a seam and restuff it until it plumps up, close the seam with an invisible ladder stitch, and replace a lost button eye. The twist is that restoring is not replacing. Owners want their plush to still look like theirs, so you read the note to learn which worn spots to keep: the bald patch on the ear she rubbed to fall asleep stays. The reward is a before-and-after photo card and the owner's reply, in a letter or a drawing. Between jobs you can rescue unclaimed and thrifted plush for a small shelf, then sell them or keep them in your own collection. It takes ReStory's restore-a-beloved-object loop and Dressmaker's hands-on craft, and points them at adult plush collecting (Jellycat and friends), a category with a huge fan culture and almost no games.
concepts.audience: Adult plush collectors and kidults (Jellycat, Squishmallows, vintage teddy fans), players who loved ReStory, PowerWash and Unpacking, and the large audience that watches plush and teddy restoration videos. Skews toward women aged 18-35, and toward parents who will share the game with children.
concepts.sessionLength: One plush takes 10-15 minutes from box to reply letter; a shift of three jobs is a natural evening stop.
concepts.artDirection: Soft, warm, slightly storybook 3D on a single workbench; plush fabrics rendered closely enough that you can tell mohair from minky.

originality.why: The restore-a-beloved-object loop is ReStory's; plush as the object and the 'keep the love marks' judgment are the fresh parts.

provenDemand.why: Restoration and before/after loops have sold many times (ReStory 500k+, House Flipper 2 1M+, PowerWash 17M players).

demand.why: Plush and teddy restoration is an evergreen satisfying-video format, and adult plush collecting is a large, very online fandom.

gap.why: Searches find only kids' mobile apps and itch.io jam games about plush repair; generalist restoration sims (The Repair House) touch toys but nobody owns plush.

soloSpeed.why: Bench-scale keeps the scope small, but soft-body restuffing, fabric shaders and the stitch interaction need careful tuning in 3D.

creatorFit.why: Needs a set of hand-made 3D plush models and wear states; that art is the main cost for one person, though the videos make themselves.

instantPlay.why: A fixed bench camera with drag-to-stitch and tap-to-tool works on a phone, but a 3D build still loads slower and runs hotter than a 2D one.

monetization.why: $14.99 premium, plush-pack DLC, and an unusually natural merch line (a real plush of the mascot bear) on top.

marketability.why: A grey, flattened childhood bear turning plump and clean next to its owner's note is a 10-second clip that makes people stop and comment.

momentum.why: Tactile restoration is 2026's breakout pattern (ReStory, Dressmaker); restoration supply is only arriving in 2026-27.

culture.why: Adult plush collecting (Jellycat, Labubu, kidult toys), nostalgia, and repair/visible-mending culture all point at this theme.

scopeFit.why: A bench-scale first-person sim is well within a small team's reach.

whyNow: Tactile restoration is the 2026 breakout pattern: ReStory sold 100k on day one and 500k+ in about 1.5 months (wnhub), and Dressmaker launched with 400k+ wishlists and recouped its budget in under 24 hours (GuruGamer).

Restoration supply is thin and generalist: Cozy Game Restoration (cartridges), The Repair House (mixed household objects) and Things Left Unsaid (2027) leave plush unclaimed (evergreen research, PCGamesN).
Cozy games still beat the Steam odds: 11% of cozy releases reach 1,000 reviews vs 4.2% of Steam overall, even with 1,041 cozy releases by late Sept 2026 (Steam Page Analyzer).
Adult plush collecting gives the game a ready-made fandom that films and shares itself, the way BookTok carried Tiny Bookshop to 500k+ copies.

Every step is a hand action you can feel: lather, shave, stuff, stitch, pull tight.

concepts.niche: First-person craft sim · pottery studio · kiln-opening reveal
concepts.oneLiner: Throw, trim and glaze pots in a small studio, then open the kiln to see how each glaze actually came out.
concepts.hook: Every kiln opening is an unboxing you made yourself.
concepts.pitch: A first-person, bench-scale pottery game. You center clay on the wheel by holding steady pressure until the wobble calms, open it, and pull the walls up in three slow passes. Push too hard and the pot slumps (which is funny, and you just start again). Leather-hard pots get trimmed, bisque-fired, then glazed by dipping, pouring and layering. You pack the kiln shelf by shelf, close the lid and wait for the firing. Then comes the clip: you lift the lid and the glazes are a little different every time. Runs, speckles, crawls, the odd rare ash drip or crystal bloom, depending on thickness, layering and where the pot sat in the kiln. Neighbours leave commission notes ('a mug big enough for my soup', 'a bowl for my late cat's water dish, to keep'), and at the weekend you sell the rest at a market stall where you price and arrange your table. Kintsugi is a side mode: people bring broken pieces and you mend them with gold seams. It is Dressmaker's hands-on craft with the TCG Card Shop pack-opening thrill built into the kiln, set in one of the biggest hobby booms on social media.

concepts.oneLiner: Run a small florist: hear each customer's story, pick stems from the buckets, hand-tie the bouquet, ribbon it, and watch them react.
concepts.hook: An apology, a first date, a funeral: say it with the right stems.
concepts.pitch: A first-person, bench-scale florist game. A customer comes to the counter with a small story: an apology to a sister, a nervous first date, a funeral for a beekeeper, a graduation. You pick stems from the buckets behind you, condition them (strip leaves below the waterline, cut at an angle under water, peel guard petals), then build a hand-tied spiral by adding each stem at an angle and turning the bunch in your hand, or arrange a vase. You wrap it in paper, pull a ribbon into a bow and tuck in a card. The customer reacts, and there is never one right answer: colour, mood, scent, season and budget all count, the way Tiny Bookshop rewards a good recommendation without a single correct book. Stock changes with the seasons. Peonies come and go, dahlias arrive late, and what you ordered at the morning flower market decides what you can say today. Regulars return, so the first-date customer may come back for an anniversary. It joins Tiny Bookshop's 'give them the right thing' with Dressmaker's hands-on craft.

concepts.name: Soak & Snooze
concepts.niche: Walk-and-restock idle-arcade management · animal hot-spring inn · web first, then Steam
concepts.oneLiner: Run a tiny mountain hot-spring inn for animals: carry towels, warm stones and tea between steaming pools until a pile of capybaras melts into the water.
concepts.pitch: Soak & Snooze takes the walk-and-restock loop that Monkey Mart and My Perfect Hotel proved on portals and phones and sets it in a small snowy onsen whose guests are animals. You are Momo, a young red panda innkeeper. You run between pools with stacks of towels on your head, top up warm stones, pour tea, hand out cold bottled milk after the bath, scrub the tubs and collect coins, then spend them on new pools, rooms and helpers. Every species has its own preference and a little ritual. Capybaras pile into the yuzu bath and doze. Snow monkeys want hot stones and a snowball afterwards. Foxes are fussy about temperature. Otters will only relax with a rubber duck. A cozy hand-painted art style and a rare venue set it apart from the low-poly look every portal clone shares. It launches free on Poki and CrazyGames, which tests the hook and pays from ads, and grows into a premium Steam game with decorating, regulars with stories, seasons and a desktop 'soak window' idle mode.
concepts.audience: Two groups. On the web: phone and school-browser players who already love Monkey Mart-style games (Poki has 100M monthly players). On Steam: cozy players who bought Maltese's Fluffy Onsen, Bear and Breakfast or Cats & Soup and want a hands-on, prettier and deeper version, plus the capybara-meme crowd on TikTok.
concepts.sessionLength: Web: 3-5 minute bites that end when a new pool unlocks. Steam: one opening shift (sunset to lanterns-out) is a short evening session, and the optional soak window runs idle beside your work.
concepts.artDirection: Hand-painted top-down 2D of a small wooden mountain inn in snow: cedar, steam, yuzu-yellow floats and round, sleepy animals.

originality.why: The loop is a straight Monkey Mart / My Perfect Hotel loop and animal onsens already exist (Fluffy Onsen, Capybara Spa, Capy Spa), so only the cozy art, multi-species rituals and portal-to-Steam plan are new.

provenDemand.why: Walk-and-restock is one of the most proven loops anywhere (Monkey Mart ~300M Poki plays, My Perfect Hotel up to $178K a week in US iOS alone), and an animal onsen already sold ~188k on Steam.

demand.why: Fluffy Onsen's 95% from 2,875 reviews and Monkey Mart's 4.6 rating from 3.79M votes show both the theme and the loop are wanted.

gap.why: Bathhouse supply is medium-low on Steam (3-4 visible games), but walk-and-restock is a commodity on portals and several small capybara-spa games already exist.

soloSpeed.why: The code (queues, stations, economy tables) is easy with AI tools; the slow part is drawing and animating each animal's soak, ritual and walk cycle.

creatorFit.why: Clips make themselves (capybara piles, towel stacks), but every new species needs commissioned sprites, so art spend grows with content.

instantPlay.why: One-thumb movement with auto-pickup and auto-drop at stations is the native control scheme of this genre on phones; a 2D build loads small.

monetization.why: Portal ads (100% of revenue on traffic you bring to Poki), then a $12.99 Steam version with species and season DLC, then mobile; Fluffy Onsen's ~$4-5 price shows the ceiling is real but modest per copy.

marketability.why: A heap of capybaras melting into a steaming pool with a rubber duck on one head reads in one second with no context.

momentum.why: Cozy releases are up 143% year on year and capybara content keeps circulating, but the capybara meme is mature rather than rising.

culture.why: Capybara and animal-onsen content is a strong internet favourite, though the capybara wave has peaked a little.

scopeFit.why: A 2D top-down management game with one venue type is well within reach of a 3-6 person studio.

whyNow: Maltese's Fluffy Onsen sold ~188k units (~$814k) at 95% positive in 2025 with only 3-4 visible bathhouse competitors; nobody has yet made the hands-on, nicely drawn version (steampulse).

Monkey Mart reached ~300M plays on Poki and reportedly cost under $10k to make, and Poki hit 1B gameplays in a month in 2025: the walk-and-restock loop has a ready audience on phones (cinevva / Poki).

Cozy games still reach 1,000 reviews at 11% against 4.2% for all of Steam, even with 1,041 cozy releases by late September 2026, and cute-animal hospitality games keep selling (Bear and Breakfast 157k-357k).

look.short: A tiny snowy mountain onsen seen from above · hand-painted 2D · cedar, steam and yuzu yellow
look.vibe: Imagine looking down through falling snow into a little wooden inn on a mountainside at dusk. Three round stone pools glow teal, wrapped in steam. In the middle one, five capybaras are piled together with their eyes closed and yuzu fruit bobbing around them; one has a yellow rubber duck on its head. A small red panda in an indigo happi coat trots between them with a wobbling tower of folded towels on its head. Paper lanterns are just coming on.
look.layout: Portrait on phones, landscape on Steam. Seen from above at a slight three-quarter angle, like looking into a dollhouse with the roof off. The inn fills the screen: an entrance gate at the bottom where guests queue, a wooden corridor up the middle, pools on either side, the towel shelf, stone brazier and tea counter along the walls. Unbought plots are shown as snowy patches with a wooden price sign that fills up as you stand on it. Coins and a small guest counter sit at the top; there are no other menus during play.
references: Monkey Mart and My Perfect Hotel for readability of stations and carry stacks (not their look)
Japanese ryokan and rural onsen photography in snow
Children's picture-book watercolour animals (soft, round, sleepy)
Cats & Soup for how cute idle animals can carry a whole game
look.shapes: Everything soft and round: pebble-shaped pools, bean-shaped animals, pillowy steam clouds, chunky timber with rounded ends. Very few sharp corners; roofs are thick and snow-capped.
look.characters: Animals drawn as simple round masses with tiny legs and big closed-eye expressions. Momo, the red panda innkeeper, has an indigo happi coat and a bushy striped tail that bobs when running. Each species has one readable silhouette and one prop: capybara + yuzu, snow monkey + hot stone, fox + little towel folded on its head, otter + rubber duck, tortoise elder + long pipe of steam.
look.camera: Fixed top-down three-quarter view that follows Momo gently; it pulls back as the inn grows so the whole place stays readable on a phone.
look.lighting: Dusk to night. Warm lantern pools of orange light on snow, teal glow from the water, steam catching the light. Each new pool you buy lights its lanterns one by one.
look.textures: Painted watercolour wash on wood and stone, soft grain on the tatami, sparkly snow edges; flat colour on characters so they stay readable at small size.
look.ui: Wooden price signs and paper tags floating over stations; coins are little copper mon with a hole; guest wishes shown as tiny thought bubbles with a single icon (towel, stone, tea, duck).
look.type: A rounded hand-lettered display font for signs and titles; a clean rounded sans for numbers. Small Japanese signage only where it is correct and checked.
look.motion: Carry stacks sway with each step; guests slowly sink into the water, ears flatten, eyes close, steam puffs rise in rhythm; coins hop out of pools in arcs to your feet.
look.sound: Water lapping, wooden footsteps, soft 'plop' as a guest sinks, wind chimes, distant snow wind; gentle koto/shamisen-flavoured lo-fi that thins out at night.
look.screenshot: A full inn at night in snow: six glowing pools, a capybara pile in the yuzu bath, monkeys on hot stones, Momo mid-run with a towel tower.
look.clip: Five capybaras slide one by one into the yuzu pool, slump into a pile, eyes close in sequence, and a rubber duck is placed on the top one's head. Then a coin shower.
avoid: Spirited Away look-alikes: towering red multi-storey bathhouse, spirits, a witch owner, bridges and trains

Stress UI: red timers, angry faces, fail screens
Generic 'Japanese' mash-ups (torii everywhere, ninja, geisha imagery)
look.artBrief: Commission one illustrator-animator for 2D top-down sprites at a three-quarter view. Each species needs: idle, walk, sink-into-water, soaking loop (eyes closed, slow breathing), its ritual, and a happy exit, all as cut-out parts that can be bone-rigged in the engine so frames stay few. Characters are round, soft, readable at 64-96 px tall on a phone. Environments come from a bought top-down Japanese interior / nature tileset repainted toward the palette; the illustrator does pools, steam, lanterns, key art and the Steam capsule. Test every new sprite by placing it in a pool pile next to a capybara: if it doesn't read as a melted, happy animal at phone size, redraw it.

concepts.niche: Cozy builder-manager · small seaside aquarium · Steam-first with a browser hook test
concepts.oneLiner: Turn an old boathouse into a tiny seaside aquarium: gather creatures from the rock pools, design glowing tanks, welcome school trips and nurse a stranded seal pup back to the sea.
concepts.pitch: Tidepool Lane is a small, warm take on the aquarium tycoon that Megaquarium has owned since 2018. You inherit a leaky boathouse in a fishing village and turn it, floor by floor, into a tiny public aquarium seen side-on like a dollhouse. At low tide you walk the rock pools to find hermit crabs, anemones and starfish; back inside you design tanks (rocks, plants, sand, light colour), keep each one's water happy with a few simple needs, open a touch pool, a jellyfish room and a café, and welcome visitors and noisy school trips. Every so often the village calls: a seal pup on the beach, a turtle caught in netting. You nurse it in the rescue pool and then release it while everyone watches from the slipway. It is honestly Steam-first. Tank design and building want a mouse and a bigger screen, and creature art is the bottleneck, so the browser version is a small hook test (one rock pool, one tank, one rescue), not a portal game.
concepts.audience: Cozy management players who liked Megaquarium, Let's Build a Zoo or Bear and Breakfast but want something gentler; aquarium-lovers and 'jellyfish ASMR' viewers; families and teachers (school trips, real marine facts); marine-rescue fans who follow seal-hospital content.

concepts.artDirection: Side-on dollhouse cutaway of a seaside boathouse aquarium in a linocut / risograph print style: inky outlines, flat sea colours and tanks that glow when lit.

gap.why: Ocean/underwater supply is 3/10 and Megaquarium is still the reference, but small idle and fishkeeping aquariums are appearing in 2026 (ARC Aquarium, Lured In, We Love Fish Tanks, Loopquarium).

soloSpeed.why: Building placement, visitor pathing, tank needs and dozens of creatures is a lot more than a station loop, and every creature needs commissioned art.

whyNow: Megaquarium (2018) is still the aquarium reference, with 3,410 Steam reviews at 95%, and it is a systems-heavy tycoon, not cozy; the research found aquarium supply 'low' (gg.deals / management research).

look.short: A seaside boathouse aquarium cut open like a dollhouse · linocut print style · tanks that glow in the dark
look.vibe: Imagine a weathered blue boathouse on a slipway, sliced open so you can see every floor at once like a dollhouse. On the ground floor, kids press their faces to a tank of orange garibaldi and swaying kelp; upstairs, a little café with mugs steaming by a round window; in the basement, a dark room where jellyfish glow pink and violet. Outside, the tide is out and the rock pools shine. Everything is printed in inky linocut lines on cream paper, and the only true light comes from the water.
look.layout: Landscape. The building is shown side-on as a cross-section filling the middle of the screen: ground floor at the waterline, café and offices above, the dark jellyfish room below, the pier and rock pools to the right, the village street to the left where visitors arrive. Tanks sit in the walls as glowing windows. You place rooms and tanks on a simple grid. A tide clock in the top corner shows when the rock pools are open; the toolbar along the bottom has rooms, tanks, decorations and the creature book.
references: Linocut and risograph prints of sea creatures (the look of a seaside print shop)
Small British, Breton and New England harbour aquariums
Jellyfish exhibit photography for the glow room
Tiny Bookshop for the warm seaside-town mood
look.shapes: Chunky print shapes with inky outlines and slight misregistration; boathouse planks, round porthole windows, arched tank frames; creatures simplified into bold, readable silhouettes.
look.characters: Visitors are small, stocky print figures with one colour accent each (a yellow raincoat, a red bobble hat); school trips are a line of matching caps with one teacher at the front. You play a keeper in rubber boots and a knitted jumper. Creatures are the stars: each has a bold silhouette, a few rigged parts and one signature motion (octopus curling, seahorse bobbing, crab sidestepping, seal rolling).
look.camera: Side-on, panning and zooming across the cutaway; a close-up mode frames a single tank full screen for designing and for photos.
look.lighting: The building is muted, printed and flat; light comes from the water. Each tank has its own glow colour that you choose, and turning on a new tank brightens the whole room. Night opening hours make the jellyfish room the brightest thing on screen.
look.textures: Paper grain over everything, visible ink texture, halftone dots in shadows, soft caustic ripples moving inside tanks.
look.ui: Tide-table and specimen-label styling: creature cards like museum labels with a print of the animal and one true fact; needs shown as three small icons on each tank (sun for warmth, droplet for clean, fish pair for neighbours).
look.type: A sturdy slab-serif for labels and signs, like a harbour notice board; a clean humanist sans for numbers.
look.motion: Fish swim in simple loops with a slight wobble; kelp sways; visitors press noses to glass and point; bubbles drift up; on release, the seal pup flops, pauses, looks back and slides into the sea.
look.sound: Bubbles and filters humming, gulls, rope creaks, rain on the roof in storms, kids' delighted gasps; a gentle score of accordion, guitar and glass harmonica.
look.screenshot: The full boathouse at dusk: the jellyfish room glowing violet below, a lit reef tank on the ground floor with a school trip in front of it, the café warm above, rock pools catching the sunset outside.
look.clip: A dark, empty tank: you place rocks, kelp and three jellyfish, press the light switch, and the tank blooms violet while a line of children turns to look. Second clip: the whole village on the slipway as a rescued seal pup slides back into the sea.
avoid: Glossy 3D aquarium realism (can't compete, too costly)
Sad or graphic injury imagery in rescues: show a bandage and a blanket, never wounds
Captivity-unease: no dolphins or whales in tanks; big animals are rescued and released
Generic cartoon 'Finding Nemo' clown fish styling
look.artBrief: Commission one illustrator who can work in a linocut / risograph style for side-view sea creatures. Each creature is drawn as 3-6 separate cut-out parts (body, fins, tail, tentacles) for bone rigging in the engine, with a palette of at most three ink colours plus paper. Start with the 8 hook-test creatures (hermit crab, shore crab, beadlet anemone, starfish, blenny, moon jellyfish, seahorse, seal pup). Environments are flat printed planes: building cross-section, rock pools, village street. Tank glow is done in code (additive light and caustics), so the illustrator never paints lighting. Check every creature at 1/4 size: the silhouette alone should name the animal.
